HAA CEO Gagan Biyani and Replit CEO Amjad Masad on the simplest way to learn anything: build something you actually want with it.

Gagan: "If you're going to learn coding at the academy, I don't want you just to take a class on Python. Go build something that you're super excited about in Python. Use it as a tool to learn the language."

"They don't need a customized syllabus or exercise given to them. They just need the freedom and confidence to say, 'Yes, you're allowed to do this. We're super excited about it.'"

"The idea that you're learning something and you don't know the utility of it is a very modern invention, and it's a very weird thing to have done in society."

"For someone like me, and I think for a lot of people that are more pragmatically minded, I'm not motivated at all by the pure pursuit of knowledge. I'm motivated by skills. What skills can it give me in order to achieve what I want to build and achieve my dreams?"

Replit co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad says many startups begin as premature optimization: founders raise money for ideas they don't care about.

"I think a lot of starting startups is premature optimization. I see it in a lot of kids now, where they're part of a group and a lot of their friends are raising a lot of money, and some of them are becoming unicorns."

"The motivation becomes envy, a really negative motivation as opposed to a positive one."

"They pre-commit to an idea they're not even interested in, raise money for it, and start pre-optimizing for some path that they haven't really reached yet. That's why I always come back to this idea of curiosity. What is actually driving you?"

"Once you find that idea that you want to dedicate your life to, or dedicate the next 10 years to, it's going to have such gravity that you're not going to be able to avoid it."

"I actively tried not to start Replit, but it exploded into a startup on its own. That's the feeling you should get: 'I guess I have to do it,' because there's so much momentum behind it."

"There's a predatory thing I've heard that happens right now where VCs go to Stanford students and give them a million dollars pre-idea... It's like the music industry... You're taking this young person and pre-committing them to something they shouldn't have committed to."

@amasad

The Bank of Japan raised rates to the highest level since 1995, and the yen fell.

The hike was 25 basis points to 1.25%, but two board members voted against it and Governor Ueda refused to sound hawkish. Traders read that as Japan blinking. The yen slid to 157 per dollar, back toward the weak end of its range.

Here is what actually matters. Even after the hike, Japan's rate sits far below the US, so the yen carry trade stays alive. That is cheap Japanese money still funding risk bets around the world. It works until Japan is forced to close the gap. When that carry trade unwinds, the selling travels straight to US stocks.

I think one of the biggest gaps in people’s understanding of scientific research today, even understanding what’s valuable/what’s the bottleneck etc. is that you  need an actual hypothesis before you can run an experiment

You need to have some actual lightning of curiosity, you have to believe there’s some logical pathway that could be true, formulate it precisely enough to be falsifiable, design an experiment that can discriminate between competing explanations, and then actually RUN THE EXPERIMENT

That’s called the scientific method. We all learned this in sixth grade but something about the power of brute forcing large data in the digital age neutered what “discovery” even means in the first place. Pattern recognition is useful, and can drive efficiency but that’s not where true “gain of functions” happen. All scientists deep down know this.

So I wouldn’t really use the awesome and divine power of the word “discovery” for what Anthropic is sharing today. If anything, to me this is yet another sign that the IPO is likely struggling.

Muse is winning at model-market fit. I haven’t seen anything it does today that ChatGPT Work couldn’t do months ago, or that Instinct or another agent couldn’t do. But using it feels different. It’s fast, smooth, and you actually want to keep using it.

A faster, cheaper model paired with a great harness makes a huge difference. For an agent taking dozens of steps to get something done, every bit of latency adds up. You feel it every time you ask for something and if it's too slow it will feel clunky and annoying.

And cost matters to the product experience too. It determines how much work you can afford to run in the background, how often the agent can check things, and how many attempts it can make. It's so obvious that they have a cheap model because they run the Feed updates hourly, they also create memories hourly too and not nightly like other agents. 

You can have the same capabilities on paper and end up with very different products. IMO that’s what I think Muse is getting right: the underlying model is very good.
